doc.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013

title: Early collectors, race records and first serious jazz fans
summary: Morgenstern says jazz was once mainly dance music; Ivy League collectors, Marshall Stearns and early writers began taking it seriously around the late 1920s, hunting race records and tracing King Oliver.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Growing up with radio, records and family listening

blocks.x: Yes, it’s quite a sea change. And of course there are still, although the ranks are dwindling, but there are musicians around who very well remember the days when it was — an audience that took jazz seriously was definitely a minority. And for most people it was something to dance to, it was something to have fun to.
Was there a point in jazz history, what point in jazz history do you think that really turned around?

Well early on I think the first people who started really taking — aside from the musicians themselves — that started taking it seriously, strangely enough, were the people, a bunch of them at Ivy League colleges who started collecting jazz records and would go out of their way to find what was then known as race records, which wasn’t a pejorative. “Race” was a term that was used by the NAACP, you know they talked about race, and so when Clarence Williams and Perry Bradford, who were really the pioneers, they were the pioneers in starting this branch of ethnic recording. There was precedent, because record labels like Columbia had a whole ethnic series, they were making Greek records, Irish records, Hebrew records, Polish records. These were marketed in stores that © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

would be frequented by the particular minority. So it was not anything, there was nothing negative about it, it was just the record companies wanting to find a market to sell things. But these people, there were people at Princeton and there was — Marshall Stearns was the founder of the Institute of Jazz Studies, at Harvard. You know they started going out to find these recordings by people like, oh, Bessie Smith and of course the Armstrong Hot Five and all, which very quickly entered the recording mainstream actually. But they were the first to — and there were people in Europe also. Robert Goffin, who was the first to write a respectable book that attempted to trace the history of the music, in 1932, two years before the much more famous Panassie. So late twenties is about when this begins. And at the Institute of Jazz Studies we have a bunch of correspondence that came from a man who is not terribly well known, because he didn’t do much in the way of writing or anything, but he was — when he was in college he was a very good pianist and he sat in with the Wolverines and knew Bix [Beiderbecke] and everything. And the people who early on tried to find out about jazz, like Charles Edward Smith, who was one of the pioneer jazz writers in this country, wrote an article called “Collecting Hot” for Esquire magazine, I think it was 1933. There is correspondence there where this man knew things about King Oliver and about Bix Beiderbecke and so on. And I’m trying to think of his name. It’s a senior moment. It will come back to me. But there are letters that these people wrote to him. And they were really fishing in the dark. Because there wasn’t anyplace, you couldn’t really go anywhere. You had to go to the musicians themselves and ask them. But there was often a question of their being accessible. And King Oliver, who was being discovered on the strength of his wonderful recordings by the Creole Jazz Band had by then, by 1930, he was off the beaten path. He was working with a band mostly down south touring in the backwoods. And his career had really gone down. So it was hard to find him to ask him. So this was all being pieced together. When Marshall Stearns decided — he was an English Lit guy, you know that’s how he made his living, he got his Ph.D. It was a Chaucer specialist from Yale. But he discovered his thesis topic, and this was an obscure Scottish poet named Robert Henderson, and he is writing a little note to somebody and he says, “I found my topic,” and gives this guy’s name and he says nobody knows anything about him, just like jazz.
